explain.text:
This is Figure 1, the plain-network comparison on CIFAR-10 (no shortcuts at all, unlike the ResNet figure you asked about before).

Both panels plot error against iterations (×10⁴). In each, the olive/yellow curve is the 20-layer plain net and the red curve is the 56-layer plain net. Around iteration 3 there's a sharp drop in both curves — that's a learning-rate decay — after which the 20-layer net settles to lower error than the 56-layer net, in both training error (left) and test error (right).

The key point, stated right in the caption and the surrounding text: the 56-layer net has *higher training error* than the 20-layer net, not just higher test error. That rules out overfitting as the explanation — if it were overfitting, the deeper net would have lower training error but worse test error. Instead both go up together, which is exactly the "degradation problem" the introduction describes: adding more layers to a plain stack makes it harder to optimize, so accuracy gets worse even on the training set itself.

ask.text: By the right edge of this crop, the 56-layer (red) test error is sitting around 13-14%, while the 20-layer (olive) has settled around 9-10%. So the 56-layer net ends roughly 4 percentage points worse despite being the deeper network — the same degradation pattern as the training curves on the left, confirming it's not just an overfitting story but a genuine optimization problem with the deeper plain net.

explain.text:
This is the full three-column diagram described in the text right after "3.3. Network Architectures."

Left: VGG-19, the reference network — a conventional stack of 3x3 convs with periodic pooling to halve spatial size, ending in three big fully-connected layers (fc 4096, fc 4096, fc 1000). 19.6 billion FLOPs.

Middle: the 34-layer plain net — the authors' own baseline, designed in VGG's spirit but leaner. It starts with a 7x7 conv (stride 2) instead of VGG's stack of small convs, uses stride-2 convs for downsampling instead of separate pooling layers in most stages, follows the rule that filter count doubles whenever feature-map size halves, and ends with global average pooling plus a single fc 1000 layer rather than three large fc layers. Much cheaper: 3.6 billion FLOPs, about 18% of VGG-19.

Right: the 34-layer residual net (ResNet-34) — identical layer-by-layer structure to the middle plain net, but with curved shortcut connections arcing over pairs of conv layers. Solid curves are identity shortcuts (used when input/output dimensions match); dotted curves appear exactly where the spatial size and filter count jump (64→128, 128→256, 256→512) — these need the projection or zero-padding option in Eqn. (2) since dimensions don't match.

The point of putting all three side by side is to show the residual net is a drop-in modification of the plain net — same depth, same FLOPs, same parameter count — with the only change being those shortcut arcs.

ask.text:
The dotted shortcuts mark the places where the shortcut connection crosses a dimension change — where the spatial feature-map size is halved and the channel count simultaneously doubles (64→128, 128→256, 256→512). Since input x and the residual output F(x) no longer have matching dimensions there, a plain identity add won't work, so the text describes two fixes: zero-pad extra channels (option A, no added parameters) or use a 1x1 projection convolution via Eqn. (2) Ws (option B). Solid shortcuts, by contrast, are plain identity connections where dimensions already match.

In this 34-layer ResNet diagram there are three dotted shortcuts, one at each of the three stage transitions (going into the 128, 256, and 512-channel stages). All the other shortcuts, spanning pairs of same-size, same-channel conv layers, are solid identity shortcuts.

explain.text:
This is the full Figure 4, both panels together, showing the actual training runs on ImageNet.

Left (plain nets): cyan is plain-18, red is plain-34. Thin lines are training error, bold lines are validation error. They track closely until the first learning-rate drop around iteration 15, after which red (34-layer) clearly sits above cyan (18-layer) and stays there — both on the thin training curves and the bold validation curves. The deeper plain net converges to roughly 32-33% versus ~30% for the 18-layer, worse despite being deeper — the degradation problem described in the text.

Right (ResNets): same color scheme, but now bold red (ResNet-34 validation) drops below bold cyan (ResNet-18) after the second rate drop around iteration 30, ending near 28% versus cyan's ~31%. The thin training curves show the same reversal. So the deeper net now trains and generalizes better, exactly the opposite ordering from the left panel.

Put side by side, the point is stark: identical depths and optimizer schedule, the only difference is the shortcut connections, and that's what turns the 34-layer network from the worse performer into the better one.

ask.text:
Both panels show two sharp step-drops, around iteration 15 and iteration 30 (x-axis is iterations ×10⁴, so roughly 150,000 and 300,000 iterations). Both curves — plain and ResNet versions — drop at the same points, since they share the same training schedule.

These are learning-rate decays. The text says the learning rate starts at 0.1 and "is divided by 10 when the error plateaus." Each time the rate drops by 10x, the optimizer takes smaller, more careful steps and error falls sharply within a short span before leveling off again. It's not something intrinsic to depth or the architecture — it's a scheduling artifact that affects all four curves at the same two moments, which is exactly why the real story is in the *gap between curves after each drop*, not the drops themselves.

ask.text: The 1202-layer curve (residual-1202) is magenta, and it settles at roughly 7–8% test error — slightly higher than the black 110-layer curve, which sits around 6.5-7%. That matches the text's reported figures of 7.93% for the 1202-layer net versus 6.43% for the 110-layer one, with the gap attributed to overfitting rather than any optimization trouble, since both curves train smoothly.

explain.text:
This is Figure 7, the one you asked about earlier — now with the actual curves visible.

Top (original layer order): std of each 3×3 layer's response, after BN, before the nonlinearity. Dashed olive/red are plain-20/plain-56; solid olive/red/black are ResNet-20/56/110. The plain nets (dashed) stay elevated, bouncing around 1-2.5 std across their depth, with plain-56 (dashed red) showing a notable bump above 2 around layer 35-40. The ResNets (solid), by contrast, drop quickly to under 1.5 and mostly hover near or below 1 for most of their length — ResNet-110 (black) especially, which spends almost its whole range near 0.8-1.0, only ticking up slightly at the very end.

Bottom (same data, sorted descending): makes the comparison cleaner — each curve ranked from largest to smallest response. The ResNet curves (solid) consistently sit below the plain curves (dashed) of comparable depth, and the deeper ResNet-110 (black) sits lowest of all for most of its length.

This supports the paper's claim: residual functions tend to have smaller magnitude than the equivalent non-residual (plain) functions, and that effect grows stronger as depth increases, since individual layers in a very deep ResNet only need to make small adjustments to the signal.

ask.text: ResNet-110 (black) has the smallest responses overall. Its sorted curve sits lowest for nearly its entire length, settling under 1.0 for most layers and tailing off to around 0.7 at the far end — lower than ResNet-20, ResNet-56, and both plain nets, which all level out higher (ResNet-56 lowest among the others, but still above black through the long flat middle stretch before its line ends around layer 55).
